paragraphs.text: A German sentence puts its verb in position two, and the ending on that verb is what tells the listener who is acting. Take the pronoun and the ending together as one unit and the whole table comes down to three shapes: -e, -st and -t.
ich koche · du kochst · er/sie/es kocht · wir kochen · ihr kocht · sie/Sie kochen

Most verbs behave exactly like {{de:kochen}}: {{de:arbeiten}} gives {{de:arbeite, arbeitest, arbeitet}} and {{de:joggen}} gives {{de:jogge, joggst, joggt}}. Only the stem under the ending changes, so one pattern buys you a whole class of verbs.

Two verbs in the box on the page bend instead. {{de:lesen}} shortens to {{de:lies}} and {{de:sprechen}} swaps its middle sound for a k, which is why {{de:du sprichst}} looks nothing like the infinitive. Say them aloud — the sound change is far easier to hear than to read.
ich lese · du liest · er/sie/es liest — ich spreche · du sprichst · er/sie/es spricht

blocks.englishBridge: In English only he, she and it change the verb; German puts an ending on every form instead.

blocks.prompt: Fill each gap with the right form of the verb in brackets.

concept.title: Verben und Personalpronomen
concept.rule: The present-tense ending is set by the pronoun: -e with ich, -st with du, -t with er/sie/es, and the bare infinitive with wir, sie and Sie.
